gweilo.e: From Cantonese 鬼佬 (gwai² lou²), from 鬼 (gwai², “ghost”) + 佬 (lou², “guy, man”).

gwan.e: From various English dialects, notably Gullah.

d.x: Do I feel more like a Hongkonger than French? Even though I might consider myself a local, I will always be seen as a gweipo, chiefly because of the colour of my skin.

gweipo.e: From Cantonese 鬼婆 (gwai² po⁴, “foreign woman”), literally "ghost woman".

A surname from Polish.

A nighttime hacker on early minicomputers.

gweep.e: Purportedly coined by hackers at the Worcester Polytechnic Institute (WPI) in 1977 and still in use through 1991. However, this entry did not appear in the Jargon File until the 1993 version 3.0.0, an edition which prompted controversy about Eric Raymond's stewardship and attention to proper attestation. The reliability of this particular addition is unclear; it was likely in use at WPI in 1991 as

Gwadar.e: Borrowed from Urdu گوادر (gvādar), itself from Baluchi گوادر (gwādar), a compound of گوات (gwát, “wind, air”) + در (dar, “door, gateway”).

d.g: A historical kingdom of Wales, in the south of the country.
A former county of South Wales, renamed in 1974 from Monmouthshire.

Gwent.e: Borrowed from Welsh Gwent, from Old Welsh Guent, from Latin Venta Silurum, a Roman colony in Britannia.

d.g: A transliteration system for Mandarin Chinese, characterized by its tonal spelling without diacritic marks.
d.x: With regard to romanization, several different systems are concurrently being used in Taiwan, including Wade-Giles, Tongyong Pinyin 通用拼音, Hanyu Pinyin 漢語拼音, and Gwoyeu Romatzyh.

Gwoyeu Romatzyh.e: From the Gwoyeu Romatzyh romanization of Mandarin 國語羅馬字 /国语罗马字 (Guóyǔ Luómǎzì).

gwop.e: Uncertain. May be a dialectal pronunciation of Spanish guapo used as a noun, thus being a doublet of wop. The attestation of the aforementioned term in English as guapo in the same sense may likely be a secondary interpretation, cf. buckaroo meaning buck (“dollar”). The acronym of George Washington On Paper is likely a backronym.

d.g: A set of unarmed combat techniques in Korean martial arts.
d.x: The 18 martial techniques begin with unarmed training, or gwonbeop, including punching, wrestling and kicking , all of which are fundamental to the higher levels of armed training.

A dweeb.
d.x:

d.g: A city in Gyeonggi Province, South Korea.

Gwangmyeong.e: Borrowed from Korean 광명(光明) (Gwangmyeong, “light”). Doublet of Kwangmyong.

d.g: Karoshi; death from overwork.
d.x: It takes Park Hyun-suk, a widow who lost her husband to gwarosa – the Korean word for death by overwork – a long time to find a photo of them together.

gwarosa.e: Borrowed from Korean 과로사 (gwarosa). Doublet of guolaosi and karoshi.

d.g: A holiday celebrated in South Korea and North Korea that commemorates the restoration of Korean independence from Japanese colonial rule.

Gwangbokjeol.e: Borrowed from Korean 광복절 (gwangbokjeol), literally meaning "the day the light returned". 복 (bok), meaning "restoration" (復), refers to Korea's independence before Japanese rule.

d.g: A community in Neath Port Talbot borough, Wales, that includes the villages of Abergwynfi, Blaengwynfi and Croeserw.

Gwynfi and Croeserw.e: Formed in 2021 on the abolition of Glyncorrwg community. Gwynfi was a county borough ward, which seems to have been renamed to match the community, however the name comes from a short stream, which gives its name to Abergwynfi and Blaengwynfi.
